prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

As I in hoary winter’s night stood shivering in the snow, Surpris’d I was with sudden heat which made my heart to glow; And lifting up a fearful eye to view what fire was near, A pretty Babe all burning bright did in the air appear; Who, scorched with excessive heat, such floods of tears did shed As though his floods should quench his flames which with his tears were fed. “Alas!” quoth he, “but newly born, in fiery heats I fry, Yet none approach to warm their hearts or feel my fire but I! My faultless breast the furnace is, the fuel wounding thorns, Love is the fire, and sighs the smoke, the ashes shame and scorns; The fuel Justice layeth on, and Mercy blows the coals, The metal in this furnace wrought are men’s defiled souls, For which, as now on fire I am to work them to their good, So will I melt into a bath to wash them in my blood.” With this he vanish’d out of sight and swiftly shrunk away, And straight I called unto mind that it was Christmas day.

outputs.L2:
On a frost-white winter night, I trembled amid the snow  
when an unexpected warmth suddenly set my heart alight.  
Glancing up in alarm to discover the source of the blaze,  
I saw a beautiful infant suspended in the air, shining with fire.  

Tormented by the fierce heat, he wept so abundantly  
that his tears seemed meant to extinguish the flames,  
though those very tears only nourished them.  

“Poor child that I am,” he cried, “I have only just been born,  
yet I suffer in this burning furnace alone.  
No one comes near to kindle love within the heart  
or to share the warmth of my fire.  

My innocent breast is the oven; piercing thorns supply its fuel.  
Love forms the flame, my sighs become its smoke,  
and disgrace and contempt remain as ashes.  
Justice piles on the fuel, while Mercy fans the glowing coals.  
The substance being refined within this furnace  
is the stained souls of humankind.  

I burn now so that they may be transformed and saved;  
later, I shall dissolve into a cleansing bath  
and wash them pure with my own blood.”  

After speaking, the child disappeared, swiftly fading from view.  
At once I remembered that the day was Christmas.
outputs.L3:
On a bitterly cold winter night, the speaker is suddenly overcome by a mysterious and intense warmth. Looking around for its source, he sees an extraordinary vision: a radiant infant suspended in the air, surrounded by flames. The child burns yet continues to weep, and his tears seem only to feed the fire rather than extinguish it.

The infant explains that the flames arise from divine love, justice, and mercy, as well as from humanity’s sinfulness and rejection of God. His suffering is therefore both an expression of love and a response to human corruption. He declares that, through his fiery sacrifice, defiled souls will be purified, while his blood will wash away the stains of sin.

When the infant disappears, the speaker understands the meaning of the vision. The burning child represents Christ, whose birth is celebrated on Christmas Day but whose future suffering and crucifixion are already foreshadowed. The vision thus unites the joy of the Nativity with the redemptive sacrifice that Christ will ultimately make for humankind.
outputs.L4:
In Robert Southwell’s poem “The Burning Babe,” the speaker experiences a startling vision on a cold winter night. Against the surrounding frost and snow, the Christ child appears not as a peaceful infant in a manger but as a blazing furnace whose intense heat transforms the air around him. This contrast between winter cold and divine fire immediately establishes the poem’s central paradox: the vulnerable newborn is also a powerful source of spiritual energy. His flames represent the immeasurable force of divine love, while his tears reveal the pain that this love requires him to endure.

The poem develops this image through a series of striking contradictions. Christ burns with love for sinful humanity, yet the water of his tears does not extinguish the fire. Instead, sorrow and love exist together, each intensifying the other. Justice and mercy also appear as complementary forces: justice supplies the fuel for the furnace, since human sin demands punishment, while mercy fans the flames, transforming judgment into redemption. Christ’s suffering therefore satisfies divine justice while also expressing God’s compassion for humankind.

Southwell further compares Christ’s redemptive work to metalworking. Human souls, damaged and corrupted by sin, are imagined as base metal placed within the furnace of Christ’s love. Through the heat of his suffering, they can be melted, purified, and remade. The image suggests that salvation is not merely forgiveness but a profound spiritual transformation. Christ willingly becomes the furnace in which sinful humanity is refined, accepting pain so that others may be restored.

The vision ultimately points forward from Christ’s birth to his Passion and Crucifixion. The infant declares that he will melt into a bath of blood in which human beings may be washed clean. Thus, the poem connects Christmas with Easter: Christ is born in order to suffer and die for humanity. When the vision disappears, the speaker realizes that it is Christmas Day, but the joy of the Nativity has been permanently joined to an awareness of sacrifice. Through its paradoxical imagery of fire and water, justice and mercy, infancy and suffering, “The Burning Babe” presents divine love as both tender and terrible—a consuming force that redeems humanity through Christ’s blood.

### “The Burning Babe”  
*Robert Southwell*

As I in hoary winter’s night stood shivering in the snow,  
Surprised I was with sudden heat, which made my heart to glow;  
And lifting up a fearful eye to view what fire was near,  
A pretty babe all burning bright did in the air appear;  
Who, scorchèd with excessive heat, such floods of tears did shed,  
As though his floods should quench his flames, which with his tears were fed.

“Alas!” quoth he, “but newly born in fiery heats I fry,  
Yet none approach to warm their hearts or feel my fire but I!  
My faultless breast the furnace is, the fuel wounding thorns,  
Love is the fire, and sighs the smoke, the ashes shame and scorns;  
The fuel Justice layeth on, and Mercy blows the coals,  
The metal in this furnace wrought are men’s defilèd souls,  
For which, as now on fire I am, to work them to their good,  
So will I melt into a bath to wash them in my blood.”

With this he vanished out of sight and swiftly shrunk away,  
And straight I callèd unto mind that it was Christmas day.
